messages.author: 22aa9e0493ccdf44
messages.subject: Summary output Standard - Scaled
parts:
Hi,

I am fitting a simple model and get the following summary output. What is standard and scaled?

Which one should I use?

 

> modell_två <- '

+ DT =~ F4 + F6 + F12

+ FE =~ F2 + F5 + F7 '

 

> fit <- cfa (modell_två, data=FoF, ordered = TRUE)

> summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

lavaan 0.6-19 ended normally after 19 iterations

 

  Estimator                                       DWLS

  Optimization method                           NLMINB

  Number of model parameters                        25

 

  Number of observations                           164

 

Model Test User Model:

                                              Standard      Scaled

  Test Statistic                                 9.905      20.708

  Degrees of freedom                                 8           8

  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.272       0.008

  Scaling correction factor                                  0.500

  Shift parameter                                            0.891

 

Regards

Ulf Larsson

messages.author: 0325c6a976085eab
messages.subject: Re: Summary output Standard - Scaled
parts:
You should probably use the scaled chi-square. This is the one that corrects for non-normality, and it's usually better, unless your sample size is small (which it might be) and your number of parameters is large (which it also might be), in which case it becomes unstable.

The fact that there is such a large difference (your scaling correction factor is small) means that you have some fairly non-
normal data. 

One thing you can do to help decide is generate some data that have a structure that fits your model and a structure that does not, and give the variables similar distributions to that which you have in the data, and see if you get the right answer out.

For example (simple example, because I'm lazy):

Here's a correct model:

library(dplyr)
library(lavaan)

set.seed(42)
n <- 164

cuts <- c(-Inf, -4, -3.5, -2.5, -1.5, Inf)

FoF <- data.frame(
    DT = rnorm(n),
    FT = rnorm(n)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    F4 = cut(FT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric(),
    F6 = cut(FT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric(),
    F12 = cut(FT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric(),
    F2 = cut(DT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric(),
    F5 = cut(DT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric(),
    F7 = cut(DT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric()
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(-DT, -FT)

modell_tva <- '
DT =~ F4 + F6 + F12
FE =~ F2 + F5 + F7 '

fit_dwls <- cfa (modell_tva, data=FoF, ordered = TRUE)
summary(fit_dwls, fit.measures = TRUE)


This gives me:

Model Test User Model:
                                              Standard      Scaled
Test Statistic                                 9.254       9.933
Degrees of freedom                                 8           8

P-value (Chi-square)                           0.321       0.270
  Scaling correction factor                                  1.011
  Shift parameter                                            0.783
    simple second-order correction                                


Looks OK. (But my scaling correction factor doesn't look like yours, because I didn't match your distribution).

Then I'll add a cross-loading:


FoF_incorrect <- data.frame(
  DT = rnorm(n),
  FT = rnorm(n)
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    F4 = cut(FT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric(),
    F6 = cut(FT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric(),
    F12 = cut(FT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric(),
    F2 = cut(DT + rnorm(n) + FT + rnorm(n) * 0.2, cuts) %>% as.numeric(), # cross-loading
    F5 = cut(DT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric(),
    F7 = cut(DT + rnorm(n), cuts) %>% as.numeric()
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(-DT, -FT)

Model Test User Model:
                                              Standard      Scaled
Test Statistic                                32.352      42.201
Degrees of freedom                                 8           8

P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000       0.000
  Scaling correction factor                                  0.780
  Shift parameter                                            0.748
    simple second-order correction                                

And that fit is considerably worse, so in this case it detected that the model was wrong.

(I used the same cuts for each variable - you might want to ensure that this matches yours.)

Jeremy

Thank you very much (and you are obviously not lazy!). I have items on a likert scale (4 alternatives), with one or two items being fairly skewed.

It looked like 5 alternatives to me from the number of parameters?

The (slightly snarky) answer is that no one has written it.  :) No one gets paid to write lavaan - I can tell you why I haven't done it: writing code and fitting models is kind of fun. Jeremy

parts:
If you would like to learn more about this topic, you can try this book:

Kline, R. B. (2023). Principles and practice of structural equation modeling (Fifth edition). The Guilford Press.

The latest edition uses lavaan for illustration, with R scripts available from the companion website:

https://www.guilford.com/companion-site/Principles-and-Practice-of-Structural-Equation-Modeling-Fifth-Edition/9781462551910

Chapter 18 is about CFA with categorical variables, with explanations about the theory behind some methods, as well as comparisons between the various fit measures. Chapter 10 has a section on assessing model fit for nonnormal variables.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai
